investorSteps.title: Registration and login
investorSteps.text: A production platform requires an account with email confirmation and credentials. This prototype has an optional community sign-in instead: you prove control of your Freighter wallet by signing a one-time challenge - no email registration, no password. The wallet is the only identity.

investorSteps.text: Document and selfie verification with a verification provider, plus AML data where required. Not implemented; no identity data is collected here.

investorSteps.title: Payment

about.title: About this project
about.p1: Blockallisto (repository rwa-crowdfund-stellar) is a personal prototype exploring tokenized crowdfunding on the Stellar network: campaign funding enforced by a Soroban smart contract, with the wider platform - accounts, verification, instruments, payments - designed and documented openly in the repository.
about.p2: It is not a company, not an authorised crowdfunding service provider, and not an offer of securities. Market framing: Portugal to the World.
about.ethicsIntro: A product-level policy for the platform this prototype explores. Issuers in the following sectors are out of scope by design:
ethicsPoints: Fossil fuels, mining and nuclear power
Genetically modified organisms and conflict-mineral-linked industries
about.ethicsNote: This is a design commitment for the project, not a claim about any live operation.
about.techText: React frontend, Node backend, Soroban (Rust) contract for escrow, Freighter wallet for signing, Stellar testnet USDC. Hosting and database run on free tiers. Details and test reports are in the repository documentation.
about.behindText: In Ancient Greece, Callisto became Ursa Major - a constellation where individual points of light join to form a greater, imperishable figure. At Blockallisto, we bring that same truth to global finance through the Stellar network. We connect small investors to fill blocks of real assets. Together, we are the democratization of investment: individual points coming together into a greater whole.

groups.title: Participation instruments
groups.intro: Instruments whose return depends on the issuer's business success: profit-participating rights and equity. Indirect participation is listed here as an ownership structure, not as a separate instrument.

groups.title: Debt instruments
groups.intro: Two generic parents - loan and bond - each issued in one of three seniority states: senior, subordinated, or seniority unspecified. Investors rank as creditors.

seniorityLabels.subordinated: Subordinated (ranks behind senior creditors in insolvency)

classes.label: Participation right / certificate
classes.summary: A right (often securitised as a participation certificate) to a profit share and to repayment of the nominal value, without the full governance rights of a shareholder.
opportunities: Share in profits without buying full equity
Often combines a base repayment claim with profit participation
risks: Profit share depends entirely on issuer performance
Can rank behind ordinary creditors
Usually illiquid until maturity
classes.suitableFor: Investors who want upside tied to business results and accept equity-like risk.

classes.label: Substanzgenussrecht
classes.summary: A participation right linked to the issuer's asset base ("substance") rather than only its annual profit. Structuring and eligible issuers vary by jurisdiction and statute.
opportunities: Participation in the issuer's asset value
Can be structured for smaller issuers where statutes allow
risks: Legal form and investor protection differ strongly by jurisdiction
May involve a trustee or vehicle between investor and issuer
Usually illiquid
classes.suitableFor: Investors comfortable with bespoke structures who read the exact contract terms first.

classes.label: Share
classes.note: A capital increase is the corporate action that creates new shares; it is not a separate instrument.
classes.summary: Direct equity in the issuing company: dividend entitlement and participation in company value, with rights set by the articles. New shares reach investors through a capital increase.
opportunities: Voting or information rights depending on share class
risks: No fixed repayment claim; dividends are not guaranteed
Total loss possible
Crowdfunding shares are usually not tradable on an exchange
classes.suitableFor: Investors with a long horizon who want ownership and accept full entrepreneurial risk.

classes.label: Indirect participation
classes.note: An ownership structure, not a distinct instrument: the investor holds the underlying participation through a vehicle or trustee, and the underlying interest decides the economics.
classes.summary: Investors participate in an SME investment indirectly - for example through a vehicle or trustee - with simplified processing.
opportunities: Access to deals that would be hard to hold directly
Simplified administration through the intermediary structure
risks: An extra layer sits between investor and issuer
Return depends on issuer performance
Terms of the vehicle govern payouts and exit
classes.suitableFor: Investors who want participation economics without holding the underlying interest directly.

classes.label: Limited partnership interest
classes.summary: An interest as limited partner in a partnership: profit and loss participation per the partnership agreement, liability limited to the contribution.
risks: Loss participation can reduce or wipe out the interest
Exit often restricted by the partnership agreement
Tax and reporting duties can be more involved
classes.suitableFor: Investors who understand partnership structures and accept entrepreneurial risk.

classes.label: Loan
classes.summary: A direct loan to the issuer with a defined interest rate and repayment schedule. The same loan parent can be senior, subordinated (including profit-participating variants), or leave seniority unspecified.
opportunities: Fixed schedule is easier to model than equity
Subordinated variants pay higher interest in exchange for the lower rank
risks: Issuer default can mean total loss
Subordinated claims are paid only after senior creditors in insolvency
No deposit protection
classes.suitableFor: Investors who accept credit risk without bank-like protection.

classes.label: Bond
classes.summary: A securitised debt instrument with a defined coupon and term. Issued senior (non-subordinated), subordinated (including explicitly subordinated qualified bonds and subordinated Mini Bonds), or with seniority unspecified.
opportunities: Senior issues rank ahead of subordinated capital and equity in insolvency
risks: Subordination raises loss severity in insolvency
Still unsecured unless collateral is stated
No participation in company growth
classes.suitableFor: Yield-oriented investors who can bear a total loss and do not need the money back early.

overlays.label: Zero-coupon (Zero Bond)
overlays.summary: A coupon structure on a loan or bond, not a seniority: no periodic interest; the return comes from issuance below nominal value and repayment at par. Combines with a debt parent, never stands alone.

overlays.label: Convertible
overlays.summary: A conversion feature on a bond: under configured terms (trigger event, exercise window, conversion price, interest-stop rules) the bond converts into shares. Combines with the bond parent, never stands alone.

qualifiers.label: "Junior"
qualifiers.summary: A lower-rank label in platform wording. It indicates subordinated ranking but does not by itself establish contractual qualified subordination.

qualifiers.label: "Qualified / qualifiziert"
qualifiers.summary: Platform wording found on loans and bonds. On bonds, do not read it as qualified subordination unless the terms themselves say subordinated.

qualifiers.label: "Mini Bond"
qualifiers.summary: Platform label for a small-denomination bond.

glossary.definition: The issuer receives the funds only if the goal is reached by the deadline; otherwise contributions are returned. The Soroban contract in this prototype enforces this on-chain.
The minimum amount an issue must raise to close. Distinct from the per-investor minimum investment.
The smallest amount one investor can subscribe, usually one unit.
A ranking rule: subordinated claims are paid only after senior creditors in insolvency, which raises the loss risk.
International Securities Identification Number. Identifies a security. This prototype issues no securities and no ISINs.
A standardised short document with the key facts and risks of an offer, required for many EU crowdfunding offers.
A window after an investment offer during which certain investors can revoke free of charge where the applicable regime requires it. Length and applicability depend on investor class and regime.
A check of an investor's understanding of crowdfunding risks that some regimes require before non-sophisticated investors can invest.
An estimate of whether an investor can bear the loss of the investment, required by some regimes for non-sophisticated investors.
Regulation (EU) 2020/1503 on European crowdfunding service providers. Authorised providers appear in the ESMA register. This prototype is not an authorised provider.
Funds held by a neutral mechanism until conditions are met. Here the campaign contract itself escrows contributions on Stellar testnet.
The smart-contract platform on the Stellar network used by this prototype.
A public test network with worthless assets, used to try software without real money.
The face value of one unit of an instrument, against which interest and repayment are calculated.
Repayment of the full nominal amount in one payment at maturity.
Day-count conventions that define how interest accrues between payment dates.
A bond with no periodic interest: it is issued below its nominal value and repaid at par, so the return is the difference. A coupon structure, not a seniority.
A bond with a conversion feature: under the issue terms (trigger, window, conversion price) it can convert into shares. A structure overlay on a bond, not a standalone instrument.
Platform wording for a lower-rank claim. It indicates subordinated ranking but does not by itself establish contractual qualified subordination.

A contractual form of subordination under which interest and sometimes principal payments stop when the issuer would become over-indebted. Platform wording such as "qualified" alone does not prove it; the terms must say subordinated.
Platform label for a small-denomination bond.
Identity verification that regulated platforms must complete before an investor can invest. This prototype performs no KYC.
A person holding a prominent public function, subject to enhanced checks under anti-money-laundering rules.
A custody view where a platform shows an investor their held securities, tied to their verified identity. This prototype holds positions in the campaign contract itself, visible per wallet.

entries.q: Is this a real investment platform?
entries.a: No. This is a technical prototype on Stellar testnet. It lists no live offers, accepts no real funds and is not an authorised crowdfunding service provider. Authorised EU providers are listed in the ESMA register.

entries.q: What do I need to try it?
entries.a: Install the Freighter wallet extension, switch it to testnet, fund it with free testnet XLM and testnet USDC from a faucet or friend, then connect it here. Testnet assets are worthless.

entries.q: Do I need my own wallet?
entries.a: Yes. This design keeps keys with the user: the Freighter wallet is the only identity and signs every transaction. The platform holds no keys and no balances of its own. Some production platforms instead custody assets through specialised partners; this prototype deliberately does not.

entries.q: Who can invest on a platform like this in production?
entries.a: A production platform must verify each investor's identity (KYC) and, where the regime requires it, test knowledge and simulate loss-bearing capacity before larger amounts. Residence restrictions can also apply. None of that exists here, because testnet funds are worthless.

entries.q: How does a contribution work?
entries.a: You pick a campaign, enter an amount and sign one transaction in Freighter. The Soroban contract escrows your contribution and enforces the funding cap atomically. The app keeps the exact signed transaction so a network error never creates a duplicate.

entries.q: Which payment methods can I use?
entries.a: Only testnet USDC sent through your Freighter wallet. There are no cards, no bank transfers and no fiat at all. A production version would settle through a licensed payment provider with a per-investment reference; that step is planned, not built.

entries.q: Can I contribute more than once to the same campaign?
entries.a: Yes. Each contribution is its own signed transaction, and the contract checks the remaining room under the funding cap on every one. An amount that would push the campaign past its goal is rejected by the contract, not by platform bookkeeping.

entries.q: What happens when a campaign reaches its goal?
entries.a: The cap is enforced by the contract, so there is no oversubscription: once the goal is met, further contributions are rejected. After the deadline has passed, the campaign creator can withdraw the escrowed funds.

entries.q: How do I check that my contribution went through?
entries.a: Connect your wallet and open the campaign page to see the escrowed totals the contract reports. Because settlement is a Stellar testnet transaction, you can also verify it independently on a public testnet explorer.

entries.q: How do refunds work?
entries.a: If a campaign misses its goal by the deadline, each contributor signs their own refund transaction. If the goal is met, only the campaign creator can withdraw, and only after the deadline.

entries.q: Can I cancel a contribution after signing?
entries.a: Not in this prototype: a signed testnet transaction is final. Cancellation is a planned step. For comparison, the EU crowdfunding regime gives non-sophisticated investors a reflection period of 4 calendar days to withdraw a binding offer on a real platform.

entries.q: Who holds the money while a campaign is running?
entries.a: The Soroban contract itself escrows contributions until the deadline. No operator account can move them: the code allows only a creator withdrawal after a successful deadline, or contributor refunds after a failed one.

entries.q: What does tokenization mean here?
entries.a: Tokenization means representing the rights and obligations of an investment digitally, so ownership and transfers can be recorded and checked on a shared ledger. This prototype takes a first step: contribution records live in a Soroban smart contract on the Stellar test network, enforced by code rather than platform bookkeeping.

entries.q: What does the smart contract actually enforce?
entries.a: Escrow of contributions, the funding cap on every transaction, the campaign deadline, all-or-nothing settlement (creator withdrawal only after a successful deadline) and contributor-signed refunds after a failed one. What it does not do is covered by the planned steps on the How it works page.

entries.q: Is there a tradable token?
entries.a: No. Contribution balances in this first contract are deliberately nontransferable. A transferable security token would need a legally recognised register, verified holders and the compliance surface described in the project documents before it could represent a real investment.

entries.q: Where are my contributions held?
entries.a: In the contract's escrow on the public test network, not with the platform operator. Your wallet keys stay in Freighter on your own device; losing them would lose access to the contribution record, exactly like any self-custody setup.

entries.q: What are the risks of real crowdfunding?
entries.a: Total loss is possible, investments are illiquid, and no deposit guarantee applies. A common rule of thumb is to invest only a small share of freely available funds and to diversify. The risk warnings page covers this in detail.

entries.q: Why should investors diversify?
entries.a: Spreading money across several projects, sectors and instrument types reduces the impact when one project fails. Concentrating everything in a single offer makes the outcome depend on one company.

entries.q: Is this platform regulated?
entries.a: No. It is not an authorised crowdfunding service provider and lists no live offers. In the EU, crowdfunding providers are authorised under the ECSPR regime and listed in the public ESMA register, which is linked in the footer of every page.

entries.q: Can I sell, gift or transfer a contribution?
entries.a: No. Contribution records in this prototype are nontransferable by design. On production platforms, transfers depend on the contractual terms of each instrument, often need issuer consent, and always require the receiving person to be identified. There is no secondary market here.

entries.q: Will transfers be possible later?
entries.a: Transfers between verified users, and possibly a bulletin-board style marketplace, are planned design steps. They need identity verification and per-instrument contractual rules first, neither of which exists in the code today.

entries.q: Do I need an account?
entries.a: No email registration and no password. An optional community sign-in proves control of your Freighter wallet by signing a one-time challenge. The wallet is the only identity, and connecting or signing never shares your keys with the site.

entries.q: What personal data does this prototype collect?
entries.a: Only what the community features store if you use them: your Stellar public key, an optional display name, and the comments, support tickets or issuer applications you submit (issuer applications may include an optional contact email). Comments are public. No full name or identity document is asked for. Your browser keeps a local record of a pending transaction so it cannot be duplicated, and the backend keeps a technical journal of requests; the Privacy Policy lists storage and retention. A production platform would have to meet GDPR duties: access, correction, erasure and portability of your data.

entries.q: Where are my contractual documents and receipts?
entries.a: Nowhere yet: document hosting and a personal portfolio are planned steps. A production platform stores the contractual documents per investment and issues a confirmation once an investment is concluded.

entries.q: Are taxes deducted from returns?
entries.a: This prototype pays no returns, so nothing is taxed or withheld. On real platforms the treatment depends on your country of residence, the instrument and the issuer's country; some providers withhold tax or issue annual certificates, and the investor stays responsible for correct declaration.

entries.q: Can I list my company today?
entries.a: You can submit an issuer application from the Financing page; the operator reviews applications off-site and nothing is listed automatically. The campaign registry currently holds only the demo campaign.

entries.q: Which financing models does the design cover?
entries.a: Four participation-side parents - participation right / certificate (with Substanzgenussrecht as a subtype), share, indirect participation as an ownership structure, and limited partnership interest - and two debt parents, loan and bond, each issued senior, subordinated or with seniority unspecified. Zero-coupon and convertible are structure overlays on debt. The Learn hub explains each.

entries.q: How would an issuer receive the funds?
entries.a: All-or-nothing: the campaign creator can withdraw the escrowed funds only if the goal is met, and only after the deadline. The rule is enforced by the smart contract, not by a platform promise.

entries.q: What would a real launch require?
entries.a: A licence path (own authorisation or a partnership with a licensed provider), a legally recognised register for each instrument and jurisdiction, payment processing through a licensed provider, KYC/AML, and the compliance pages and documents described in the project docs. These are open decisions, not implemented features.

entries.q: What does it cost?
entries.a: The prototype runs on free-tier hosting and testnet infrastructure. No fee model for issuers or investors is defined or charged.

blogPosts.title: What Blockallisto is - and what it is not
paragraphs: Blockallisto is a working prototype for tokenised crowd investing on the Stellar testnet. It explores how a transparent investment platform could work: public campaign terms, on-chain contribution tracking and enforceable refund rules.

It is not an investment platform. There are no live offers, no real funds and no investment advice anywhere on this site. Every campaign runs on the Stellar testnet, and testnet assets are worthless by design.
What is real is the machinery: the smart contracts, the wallet flows and this website operate with valueless test assets while the prototype is exercised and improved.

blogPosts.title: How a campaign works end to end
paragraphs: Each campaign is a Soroban smart contract with a goal and a deadline. Visitors connect a Freighter wallet and contribute testnet USDC; every confirmed contribution is visible on chain and in the campaign progress bar.

The contract enforces the outcome without a middleman: once the deadline has passed, the creator can withdraw only if the goal was reached. If the campaign ends below its goal, each contributor signs their own refund and takes their contribution back.
Your own positions, activity and notifications live under My account once you connect a wallet - saved per wallet, on the server, not in a cookie.

blogPosts.title: Why a demo has legal pages
paragraphs: This prototype borrows its structure from real crowd-investing regulation. The EU regulates crowdfunding under ECSPR, and authorised providers appear in the ESMA register; Blockallisto is not an authorised provider and lists no live offers.

Pages such as Risk Warnings, Conflicts of Interest, Complaints Management and Business Continuity exist here as illustrative templates marked [DEMO]. They show the transparency a real platform must provide - they are not legal documents and have not been reviewed by a lawyer.
The same rule applies everywhere on this site: fictional particulars are marked [DEMO], and nothing here may be quoted as a real company statement.

catQuestions.q: What is the most you can lose with a crowdfunding investment?
catQuestions.why: Crowdfunding investments can lose their entire value (total loss).

catQuestions.q: How easily can you usually sell a crowdfunding investment?
options: Any time on a stock exchange
Only at the end of the year
catQuestions.why: There is generally no secondary market; plan to hold until the end of the term.

catQuestions.q: Who bears the loss if the issuing company fails?
catQuestions.why: The investment is a contract with the issuer; the platform does not cover losses.
Spreading investments reduces the impact of a single total loss.

catQuestions.q: Are returns on crowdfunding investments guaranteed?
catQuestions.why: Interest and repayment depend on the issuer; no return is guaranteed.
